claims.evidence: This is part of the formal diagnosis of Sauropterygomorpha based on phylogenetic analysis.

claims.claim: Sauropterygomorpha is diagnosed by metatarsal I being less than 50% the length of metatarsal IV.
claims.source: Diagnosis: Osteoderms present (ch. 143.1), body strongly flattenned dorso-ventrally (ch. 144.1), clavicle applied to the medial surface of scapula (ch. 148.1), metatarsal V long and slender (ch. 186.0), metatarsal I less than 50% the length of metatarsal IV (ch. 189.1).
claims.evidence: This is part of the formal diagnosis of Sauropterygomorpha based on phylogenetic analysis.

claims.claim: The holotype of Prosaurosphargis yingzishanensis is HFUT YZSB-19-109, a partial postcranial skeleton.
claims.source: Holotype: HFUT YZSB-19-109, a partial postcranial skeleton (Figure 2).
claims.evidence: This is the formal designation of the holotype specimen.

claims.claim: The specimen is housed in the Geological Museum of Hefei University of Technology, Hefei, Anhui Province, China.
claims.source: The specimen is housed in the Geological Museum of Hefei University of Technology, Hefei, Anhui Province, China (HFUT).
claims.evidence: This is factual information about the specimen repository.

claims.claim: The genus name Prosaurosphargis is derived from the Greek preposition πρό (pró), meaning before, and Saurosphargis.
claims.source: Etymology: Genus name from the Greek preposition πρό (pró), meaning before, and Saurosphargis, the name of the type genus of the family Saurosphargidae (Li et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This is the formal etymology of the genus name.

claims.claim: The specific epithet yingzishanensis refers to the type locality.
claims.source: The specific epithet refers to the type locality (see above).
claims.evidence: This is the formal etymology of the specific epithet.

claims.claim: Prosaurosphargis yingzishanensis is from the Third Member of the Jialingjiang Formation (uppermost Spathian, Olenekian, Lower Triassic), Yingzishan quarry, Yuan'an County, Hubei Province, China.
claims.source: Horizon and locality: Third Member of the Jialingjiang Formation (uppermost Spathian, Olenekian, Lower Triassic), Yingzishan quarry, Yuan'an County, Hubei Province, China.
claims.evidence: This is the formal stratigraphic and geographic information for the holotype.

claims.claim: Prosaurosphargis has spaces between dorsal transverse processes anteroposteriorly shorter than the anteroposterior widths of the transverse processes.
claims.source: Diagnosis: A saurosphargid characterised by the following combination of character states: (1) spaces between dorsal transverse processes anteroposteriorly shorter than the anteroposterior widths of the transverse processes (like in Saurosphargis and Sinosaurosphargis, but different from Largocephalosaurus, in which the spaces between the dorsal transverse processes are wider than the transverse processes)
claims.evidence: This is part of the formal diagnosis based on specimen observation.

claims.claim: Prosaurosphargis has ribs without uncinate processes.
claims.source: (2) ribs without uncinate processes (like in Sinosaurosphargis, but unlike in Saurosphargis and Largocephalosaurus, in which uncinate processes are present)
claims.evidence: This is part of the formal diagnosis based on specimen observation.

claims.claim: Prosaurosphargis has osteoderms forming a median, parasaggital and lateral rows.
claims.source: (3) osteoderms forming a median, parasaggital and lateral rows (similar to Largocephalosaurus polycarpon, but different from L. qianensis, in which additional, small osteoderms more extensively cover the lateral sides of the body, and different from Sinosaurosphargis, in which the osteoderms form an extensive dorsal armour)
claims.evidence: This is part of the formal diagnosis based on specimen observation.

claims.claim: Prosaurosphargis has an ectepicondylar groove on the humerus.
claims.source: (4) ectepicondylar groove on humerus present (like in Largocephalosaurus qianensis, absent in L. polycarpon)
claims.evidence: This is part of the formal diagnosis based on specimen observation.

claims.claim: Prosaurosphargis has an entepicondylar foramen in the humerus absent.
claims.source: (5) entepicondylar foramen in humerus absent (as in Largocephalosaurus) (details of humerus morphology unknown in Sinosaurosphargis)
claims.evidence: This is part of the formal diagnosis based on specimen observation.

claims.claim: Prosaurosphargis has a radius short relative to humerus compared with other saurosphargids.
claims.source: (6) radius short relative to humerus compared with other saurosphargids
claims.evidence: This is part of the formal diagnosis based on specimen observation and comparison.

claims.claim: Prosaurosphargis has a single distal tarsal (distal tarsal IV).
claims.source: (7) presence of a single distal tarsal (distal tarsal IV) (different from Largocephalosaurus, which possesses two distal tarsals – III and IV) (number of tarsals unknown in Sinosaurosphargis)
claims.evidence: This is part of the formal diagnosis based on specimen observation.

claims.claim: Prosaurosphargis has anterior caudal ribs shorter than sacral ribs.
claims.source: (8) anterior caudal ribs shorter than sacral ribs (anterior caudal ribs longer than sacral ribs in Largocephalosaurus, unknown in Sinosaurosphargis).
claims.evidence: This is part of the formal diagnosis based on specimen observation.

claims.claim: Based on humerus:total body length and femur:total body length ratios, the total length of HFUT YZSB-19-109 is estimated to have reached between 1468 mm to 1583 mm.
claims.source: Based on the humerus:total body length and femur:total body length ratios of the type specimen of Largocephalosaurus qianensis (specimen IVPP V 15638, total body length = 2317 mm; Li et al., 2014), the only completely preserved saurosphargid specimen discovered to date, the total length of HFUT YZSB-19-109 is estimated to have reached between 1468 mm to 1583 mm, respectively.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on comparison with Largocephalosaurus qianensis.

claims.claim: The transverse processes of cervical neural arches extend posterolaterally and are proportionally shorter than the transverse processes of the dorsal neural arches.
claims.source: The transverse processes of the cervical neural arches extend posterolaterally and are proportionally shorter than the transverse processes of the dorsal neural arches.
claims.evidence: This is based on direct observation of the specimen.

claims.claim: The dorsal centrum is mediolaterally constricted at its anteroposterior mid-length, resembling the dorsal centra of other saurosphargids.
claims.source: It is mediolaterally constricted at its anteroposterior mid-length, resembling the dorsal centra of other saurosphargids (Huene, 1936; Li et al., 2011; Li et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is based on direct observation and comparison with other saurosphargids.

claims.claim: The maximum width of the transverse process is greater than the maximum width of the space between the transverse processes of adjacent neural arches.
claims.source: The maximum width of the transverse process is greater than the maximum width of the space between the transverse processes of adjacent neural arches (Figure 3), a condition similar to that exhibited by Saurosphargis (Huene, 1936) and Sinosaurosphargis (Li et al., 2011), but different from Largocephalosaurus (Li et al., 2014) and Eusaurosphargis (Scheyer et al., 2017), in which the widths of the spaces between the dorsal transverse processes are approximately equal or greater than the widths of the transverse processes.
claims.evidence: This is based on direct observation of the specimen (Figure 3) and comparison with other taxa.

claims.claim: Articulated anterior and posterior dorsal neural arches preserved without their respective centra indicate a lack of fusion of the neurocentral suture.
claims.source: Articulated anterior and posterior dorsal neural arches preserved without their respective centra indicate a lack of fusion of the neurocentral suture, a paedomorphic feature characteristic for Sauropterygia (Rieppel, 2000a) and also present in Saurosphargis (Huene, 1936) and Largocephalosaurus (Li et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is based on direct observation and comparison with other taxa.

claims.claim: Lack of fusion of the neurocentral suture is a paedomorphic feature characteristic for Sauropterygia.
claims.source: Articulated anterior and posterior dorsal neural arches preserved without their respective centra indicate a lack of fusion of the neurocentral suture, a paedomorphic feature characteristic for Sauropterygia (Rieppel, 2000a) and also present in Saurosphargis (Huene, 1936) and Largocephalosaurus (Li et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Rieppel, 2000a.

claims.claim: The caudal centra have concave lateral and ventral surfaces and are likely amphicoelus.
claims.source: The sacral and caudal centra have concave lateral and ventral surfaces and are likely amphicoelus, as evidenced by the concave anterior articular surface of the second caudal centrum
claims.evidence: This is based on direct observation of the specimen.

claims.claim: A slightly rugose/striated dorsal surface is present in some of the anterior caudal neural spines, reminiscent of a similar surface present in the dorsal neural spines of Helveticosaurus, Augustasaurus, Nothosaurus, and Pomolispondylus.
claims.source: A slightly rugose/striated dorsal surface, reminiscent of a similar surface present in the dorsal neural spines of Helveticosaurus (Rieppel, 1989a), Augustasaurus (Sander et al., 1997), Nothosaurus (Klein et al., 2022), and Pomolispondylus (Cheng et al., 2022), is preserved in some of the anterior caudal neural spines.
claims.evidence: This is based on direct observation and comparison with other taxa.

claims.claim: The anterior dorsal ribs have a single head and greatly expanded distal portions that abut against each other, forming a characteristic 'rib-basket'.
claims.source: They have a single head and greatly expanded distal portions that abut against each other, forming a characteristic 'rib-basket' also present in other saurosphargids (Huene, 1936; Li et al., 2011; Li et al., 2014), but differ from the dorsal ribs of Eusaurosphargis, which are narrow and widely spaced (Scheyer et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is based on direct observation and comparison with other taxa.

claims.claim: The dorsal ribs do not bear a distinct uncinate process, being similar to Sinosaurosphargis but different from Largocephalosaurus, Saurosphargis, Eusaurosphargis and a possible isolated saurosphargid rib from the Late Triassic of Switzerland.
claims.source: The dorsal ribs do not bear a distinct uncinate process, being similar in this respect to the dorsal ribs of Sinosaurosphargis (Li et al., 2011), but differ from the dorsal ribs of Largocephalosaurus, Saurosphargis, Eusaurosphargis and a possible isolated saurosphargid rib from the Late Triassic of Switzerland, all of which possess uncinate processes (Li et al., 2014; Scheyer et al., 2017; Scheyer et al., 2022).
claims.evidence: This is based on direct observation and comparison with other taxa.

claims.claim: The anterior caudal ribs in HFUT YZSB-19-109 are shorter than the sacral ribs, in contrast to Largocephalosaurus.
claims.source: The anterior caudal ribs in HFUT YZSB-19-109 are shorter than the sacral ribs, in contrast to Largocephalosaurus, in which the anterior caudal ribs are longer than the sacral ribs (Li et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is based on direct observation and comparison with Largocephalosaurus.

claims.claim: Each gastral rib in HFUT YZSB-19-109 was composed of five elements – a median element, two lateral (first lateral) elements and two lateralmost (second lateral) elements.
claims.source: Like in Eusaurosphargis, Placodus and eosauropterygians (Drevermann, 1933; Rieppel, 1989b; Nosotti and Rieppel, 2003; Shang et al., 2011), each gastral rib was composed of five elements – a median element, two lateral (first lateral) elements and two lateralmost (second lateral) elements.
claims.evidence: This is based on direct observation and comparison with other taxa.

claims.claim: The scapula of HFUT YZSB-19-109 closely resembles the scapula of Largocephalosaurus and Corosaurus in general shape and proportions.
claims.source: In general shape and proportions, the scapula of HFUT YZSB-19-109 closely resembles the scapula of Largocephalosaurus (Cheng et al., 2012; Li et al., 2014) and Corosaurus (Storrs, 1991)
claims.evidence: This is based on direct observation and comparison with other taxa.

claims.claim: The coracoid of HFUT YZSB-19-109 closely resembles the coracoid of Largocephalosaurus.
claims.source: The preserved parts of both coracoids indicate that it was a dorsoventrally flat, plate-like element, approximately sub-circular in outline, closely resembling the coracoid of Largocephalosaurs (Li et al., 2014; Figure 7).
claims.evidence: This is based on direct observation and comparison with Largocephalosaurus.

claims.claim: The coracoid of HFUT YZSB-19-109 differs from the coracoids of Helveticosaurus, Eusaurosphargis, Atopodentatus, early diverging placodonts, Majiashanosaurus, a referred specimen of Hanosaurus, and Lariosaurus sanxiaensis.
claims.source: The coracoid of HFUT YZSB-19-109 differs, however, from the coracoids of Helveticosaurus (Rieppel 1989), Eusaurosphargis, Atopodentatus, early diverging placodonts, Majiashanosaurus, a referred specimen of Hanosaurus, and Lariosaurus sanxiaensis, in which the coracoid is proximodistally more elongate and approximately sub-oval in outline (Figure 7).
claims.evidence: This is based on direct observation and comparison with other taxa.

claims.claim: The humerus of HFUT YZSB-19-109 is posteriorly curved along its proximodistal axis, like the humerus of other saurosphargids, Placodus, Majiashanosaurus, Lariosaurus sanxiaensis, a referred specimen of Hanosaurus and numerous eosauropterygians.
claims.source: The humerus is proximodistally elongate; it is also posteriorly curved along its proximodistal axis, like the humerus of other saurosphargids (Li et al., 2011; Li et al., 2014; Cheng et al., 2012), Placodus (Jiang et al., 2008), Majiashanosaurus (Jiang et al., 2014), Lariosaurus sanxiaensis (Li and Liu, 2020), a referred specimen of Hanosaurus (Wang et al., 2022) and numerous eosauropterygians (Rieppel, 1994).
claims.evidence: This is based on direct observation and comparison with other taxa.

claims.claim: The anterior margin of the humerus in HFUT YZSB-19-109 is not convex, but straight, making it more similar to the humeri of Placodus and Nothosaurus.
claims.source: However, in contrast to Largocephalosaurus, the anterior margin of the humerus is not convex, but straight, making it more similar to the humeri of Placodus and Nothosaurus (Rieppel, 1994).
claims.evidence: This is based on direct observation and comparison with other taxa.

claims.claim: The radius/humerus proximodistal length ratio in HFUT YZSB-19-109 is ~0.55.
claims.source: The radius/humerus proximodistal length ratio in HFUT YZSB-19-109 is ~0.55, in line with Eusaurosphargis (~0.51–0.57; Scheyer et al., 2017) and Placodus (~0.56; Jiang et al., 2008), but is significantly smaller than the ratio in Sinosaurosphargis (~0.66; Li et al., 2011), Largocephalosaurus polycarpon (~0.74; Cheng et al., 2012), L. qianensis (~0.67–0.72; Li et al., 2014), a referred specimen of Hanosaurus (~0.67; Wang et al., 2022), and Majiashanosaurus (~0.74; Jiang et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is based on measurements of the specimen and comparison with other taxa.

claims.claim: HFUT YZSB-19-109 had a proportionally shorter forearm compared with other saurosphargids and early eosauropterygians.
claims.source: This indicates that HFUT YZSB-19-109 had a proportionally shorter forearm compared with other saurosphargids and early eosauropterygians.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the radius/humerus ratio comparison.

claims.claim: The ilium of HFUT YZSB-19-109 is very similar to the ilia of Largocephalosaurus, Eusaurosphargis, Placodus, and Corosaurus.
claims.source: The ilium of HFUT YZSB-19-109 is very similar to the ilia of Largocephalosaurus (Li et al., 2014), Eusaurosphargis (Nosotti and Rieppel, 2003), Placodus (Rieppel, 1995), and Corosaurus (Storrs, 1991), which all possess a well-developed, posteriorly projecting iliac blade.
claims.evidence: This is based on direct observation and comparison with other taxa.

claims.claim: The pubis of HFUT YZSB-19-109 resembles the pubis of Largocephalosaurus in outline and proportions.
claims.source: The pubis of HFUT YZSB-19-109 resembles the pubis of Largocephalosaurus (Li et al., 2014) in outline and proportions.
claims.evidence: This is based on direct observation and comparison with Largocephalosaurus.

claims.claim: The humerus/femur ratio in HFUT YZSB-19-109 is ~1.19.
claims.source: The humerus/femur ratio in HFUT YZSB-19-109 is ~1.19, which is similar to the ratio in Largocephalosaurus (~1.20; Li et al., 2014), but is significantly greater than the ratio in Helveticosaurus (~1.11; Rieppel 1989), Placodus (~1.05; Jiang et al., 2008), and Eusaurosphargis (~0.89; Scheyer et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is based on measurements of the specimen and comparison with other taxa.

claims.claim: The phylogenetic analysis recovered 48 most parsimonious trees (MPTs) of 1008 steps each (CI = 0.272, RI = 0.620).
claims.source: The phylogenetic analysis recovered 48 most parsimonious trees (MPTs) of 1008 steps each (CI = 0.272, RI = 0.620) (Figure 8).
claims.evidence: This is the result of the phylogenetic analysis.

claims.claim: Prosaurosphargis was recovered as a member of Saurosphargidae, forming a polytomy with Sinosaurosphargis and Largocephalosaurus.
claims.source: Prosaurosphargis was recovered as a member of Saurosphargidae, forming a polytomy with Sinosaurosphargis and Largocephalosaurus.
claims.evidence: This is the result of the phylogenetic analysis.

claims.claim: Saurosphargidae is supported by three unambiguous synapomorphies: dorsal ribs transversely broadened and in antero-posterior contact with each other, forming closed 'rib-basket'; lateral gastralia expanded and flat; distal end of ulna distinctly expanded.
claims.source: Saurosphargidae is supported by the following three unambiguous synapomorphies: dorsal ribs transversely broadened and in antero-posterior contact with each other, forming closed 'rib-basket' (char. 135.1); lateral gastralia expanded and flat (char. 141.1); distal end of ulna distinctly expanded (char. 167.1).
claims.evidence: This is the result of the phylogenetic analysis.

claims.claim: Saurosphargidae was recovered within Sauropterygia, as the sister-group to the lineage leading to Eosauropterygia.
claims.source: Saurosphargidae was recovered within Sauropterygia, as the sister-group to the lineage leading to Eosauropterygia.
claims.evidence: This is the result of the phylogenetic analysis.

claims.claim: The saurosphargid-eosauropterygian clade is supported by six unambiguous synapomorphies.
claims.source: The saurosphargid-eosauropterygian clade is supported by six unambiguous synapomorphies: frontal, butterfly-shaped with antero- and postero-lateral processes absent (ch. 29.0); long postorbital posterior process contacting squamosal (ch. 32.0); mandibular articulations displaced to a level distinctly behind occipital condyle (ch. 87.1); neural canal evenly proportioned (ch. 122.0); three sacral ribs (ch. 130.1); total number of carpal ossifications more than three (ch. 194.0).
claims.evidence: This is the result of the phylogenetic analysis.

claims.claim: Pomolispondylus was recovered as the most basal member of the grade leading to Eosauropterygia.
claims.source: Pomolispondylus, recently proposed as a sister-taxon of Saurosphargidae (Cheng et al., 2022), was recovered as the most basal member of the grade leading to Eosauropterygia
claims.evidence: This is the result of the phylogenetic analysis.

claims.claim: The type and referred specimens of Hanosaurus were not unambiguously recovered in a monophyletic group.
claims.source: The type (Rieppel, 1998a) and referred (Wang et al., 2022) specimens of Hanosaurus were not unambiguously recovered in a monophyletic group
claims.evidence: This is the result of the phylogenetic analysis.

claims.claim: Corosaurus was recovered as the earliest-diverging member of Eosauropterygia.
claims.source: Corosaurus was recovered as the earliest-diverging member of Eosauropterygia
claims.evidence: This is the result of the phylogenetic analysis.

claims.claim: Wumengosaurus was recovered outside of the clade comprising pachypleurosaurs, nothosaurs and pistosaurs.
claims.source: whereas Wumengosaurus was recovered outside of the clade comprising pachypleurosaurs, nothosaurs and pistosaurs.
claims.evidence: This is the result of the phylogenetic analysis.

claims.claim: Atopodentatus was recovered as the sister-taxon of placodonts within Placodontiformes.
claims.source: The herbivorous sauropterygian Atopodentatus was recovered as the sister-taxon of placodonts (represented in our dataset by Paraplacodus and Placodus) within Placodontiformes
claims.evidence: This is the result of the phylogenetic analysis.

claims.claim: Placodontiformes is supported by four unambiguous synapomorphies: contact of the prefrontal and postfrontal excluding frontal from dorsal orbital margin; interpterygoid vacuity absent; splenial entering mandibular symphysis; and femur internal trochanter well developed.
claims.source: supported by four unambiguous synapomorphies: contact of the prefrontal and postfrontal excluding frontal from dorsal orbital margin (char. 21.1); interpterygoid vacuity absent (char. 81.1); splenial entering mandibular symphysis (char. 88.0); and femur internal trochanter well developed (char. 203.0).
claims.evidence: This is the result of the phylogenetic analysis.

claims.claim: Palatodonta was recovered as the sister-taxon of Eusaurosphargis.
claims.source: Palatodonta was recovered as the sister-taxon of Eusaurosphargis.
claims.evidence: This is the result of the phylogenetic analysis.

claims.claim: The clade comprising Palatodonta + Eusaurosphargis was recovered as the sister-group to Sauropterygia within Sauropterygomorpha.
claims.source: The clade comprising Palatodonta + Eusaurosphargis was recovered as the sister-group to Sauropterygia within Sauropterygomorpha tax. nov. (see above).
claims.evidence: This is the result of the phylogenetic analysis.

claims.claim: Helveticosaurus was recovered as the sister-group of Sauropterygomorpha.
claims.source: Helveticosaurus was recovered as the sister-group of Sauropterygomorpha
claims.evidence: This is the result of the phylogenetic analysis.

claims.claim: The clade comprising Helveticosaurus + Sauropterygomorpha is supported by six unambiguous synapomorphies.
claims.source: the clade comprising Helveticosaurus + Sauropterygomorpha is supported by the following six unambiguous synapomorphies: preorbital and postorbital regions of skull of subequal length (ch. 1.0); transverse processes of neural arches of the dorsal region distinctly elongated (ch. 124.1); scapula with a constriction separating a ventral glenoidal portion from a posteriorly directed dorsal wing (ch. 154.2); distal tarsal I absent (ch. 184.1); total number of tarsal ossifications less than four (ch. 192.1); total number of carpal ossifications two (char. 194.2).
claims.evidence: This is the result of the phylogenetic analysis.

claims.claim: Within Diapsida, the clade comprising Helveticosaurus + Sauropterygomorpha was recovered as forming a clade with Ichthyosauromorpha, Thalattosauria and Archosauromorpha.
claims.source: Within Diapsida, the clade comprising Helveticosaurus + Sauropterygomorpha was recovered as forming a clade with Ichthyosauromorpha, Thalattosauria and Archosauromorpha, a result similar to that recovered in some other recent broad-scale analyses of diapsid phylogenetic interrelationships (Chen et al., 2014a; Neenan et al., 2015; Martínez et al., 2021; Simões et al., 2022).
claims.evidence: This is the result of the phylogenetic analysis and comparison with other studies.

claims.claim: Sauropterygomorpha, Ichthyosauromorpha, Thalattosauria, Archosauromorpha, and Testudines were recovered within a monophyletic Archelosauria.
claims.source: The three major marine reptile clades (Sauropterygomorpha, Ichthyosauromorpha and Thalattosauria), Archosauromorpha, and Testudines were recovered within a monophyletic Archelosauria
claims.evidence: This is the result of the phylogenetic analysis.

claims.claim: Archelosauria is supported by four unambiguous synapomorphies: frontal with distinct posterolateral processes, frontal anterior margins oblique, forming an angle of at least 30 degrees with long axis of the skull, interclavicle anterior process or triangle conspicuously present, and upper temporal fossae present and distinctly smaller than the orbit.
claims.source: supported by four unambiguous synapomorphies – frontal with distinct posterolateral processes (ch. 26.1), frontal anterior margins oblique, forming an angle of at least 30 degrees with long axis of the skull (ch. 27.1), interclavicle anterior process or triangle conspicuously present (ch. 157.0), and upper temporal fossae present and distinctly smaller than the orbit (ch. 207.3).
claims.evidence: This is the result of the phylogenetic analysis.

claims.claim: Prosaurosphargis extends the fossil record of Saurosphargidae back by approximately 3 Ma from the Middle (Pelsonian) to the Early (Olenekian) Triassic.
claims.source: Prosaurosphargis represents the stratigraphically oldest occurrence of Saurosphargidae, extending their fossil record back by approximately 3 Ma from the Middle (Pelsonian) to the Early (Olenekian) Triassic (Figure 9).
claims.evidence: This is based on stratigraphic data and comparison with other saurosphargid occurrences.

claims.claim: Saurosphargids are the fourth major marine reptile lineage known from the Early Triassic Nanzhang-Yuan'an fauna.
claims.source: Saurosphargids are thus the fourth major marine reptile lineage known from the Early Triassic Nanzhang-Yuan'an fauna, which also includes as many as seven species of hupehsuchians (Chen et al., 2016a; Qiao et al., 2019), one species of ichthyosauriforms (Chen et al., 2013), and three taxa representing the sauropterygian lineage leading to Eosauropterygia – Hanosaurus, Lariosaurus sanxiaensis, and Pomolispondylus (Young, 1965; Rieppel, 1998a; Li and Liu, 2020; Cheng et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2022).
claims.evidence: This is based on the fossil record and citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: Prosaurosphargis is one of the larger marine reptiles known from the Nanzhang-Yuan'an fauna, measuring approximately 1.5 m in total body length.
claims.source: Measuring approximately 1.5 m in total body length, Prosaurosphargis is one of the larger marine reptiles known from this ecosystem, smaller only than a large unidentified eosauropterygian (body length of 3–4 m; Chen et al., 2014b, Chen et al., 2016a) and an indeterminate hupehsuchian (body length of ~2.3 m; Qiao et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is based on body size estimates and comparison with other fauna members.

claims.claim: The presence of several marine reptiles representing a broad range of body sizes in the Nazhang-Yuan'an fauna supports the view of a rapid diversification of predators in the immediate aftermath of the PTME and high predation pressure in shallow marine ecosystems in the Early Triassic.
claims.source: The presence in the Nazhang-Yuan'an fauna of several marine reptiles representing a broad range of body sizes (~0.25–4.00 m; Chen et al., 2014b; Qiao et al., 2019) and displaying various ecomorphological adaptations supports the view of a rapid diversification of predators in the immediate aftermath of the PTME and high predation pressure in shallow marine ecosystems in the Early Triassic (Chen et al., 2014b; Chen et al., 2014c; Li and Liu, 2020).
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the diversity and body size range of marine reptiles in the fauna.

claims.claim: Eusaurosphargis and Palatodonta likely represent the morphology of the last common terrestrial ancestor of sauropterygians.
claims.source: Our phylogenetic analysis suggests that Eusaurosphargis and Palatodonta likely represent the morphology of the last common terrestrial ancestor of sauropterygians
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the phylogenetic analysis results.

claims.claim: The status of Eusaurosphargis + Palatodonta as the sister-group to Sauropterygia is corroborated by the presence in Eusaurosphargis of morphological features otherwise known exclusively in sauropterygians: a clavicle applied to the medial surface of the scapula and a pectoral fenestration.
claims.source: The status of Eusaurosphargis + Palatodonta as the sister-group to Sauropterygia is corroborated by the presence in Eusaurosphargis of morphological features otherwise known exclusively in sauropterygians: a clavicle applied to the medial surface of the scapula and a pectoral fenestration (Scheyer et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Scheyer et al., 2017 and morphological comparison.

claims.claim: Eusaurosphargis and Sauropterygia share a similar foot morphology with metatarsal I being proximodistally much shorter than metatarsal IV and metatarsal V being long and slender.
claims.source: Furthermore, Eusaurosphargis and Sauropterygia also share a similar foot morphology with metatarsal I being proximodistally much shorter than metatarsal IV and metatarsal V being long and slender (see above).
claims.evidence: This is based on morphological comparison.

claims.claim: Helveticosaurus likely convergently evolved an aquatic lifestyle.

results.result: The authors describe a new saurosphargid species, Prosaurosphargis yingzishanensis gen. et sp. nov., from the Early Triassic (Olenekian) of South China based on specimen HFUT YZSB-19-109. The specimen is diagnosed by a combination of morphological features including dorsal rib arrangement, absence of uncinate processes, osteoderm patterns, humerus morphology, and limb proportions. The specimen is estimated to have been 1.5-1.6 m in total body length.
results.evaluation: The morphological description is detailed and supported by direct observation of the fossil specimen (C77-C97), photographic documentation (Figures 2-7), and comparative analysis with other saurosphargids. The formal diagnosis (C68-C75) provides clear distinguishing features. The specimen repository and stratigraphic context are documented (C63-C67). The body size estimate (C76) is based on established scaling relationships with a well-preserved comparative specimen.

results.result: Phylogenetic analysis recovers Saurosphargidae as nested within Sauropterygia, forming a clade with Eosauropterygia to the exclusion of Placodontia. Prosaurosphargis is recovered as a member of Saurosphargidae. The analysis produced 48 most parsimonious trees of 1008 steps each, with Saurosphargidae supported by three synapomorphies and the saurosphargid-eosauropterygian clade supported by six synapomorphies.
results.evaluation: The phylogenetic analysis is methodologically sound (C165-C169), using a comprehensive data matrix with 57 OTUs and 221 characters. The placement of Saurosphargidae within Sauropterygia is supported by multiple synapomorphies (C100, C102) and is consistent with the morphological evidence. The analysis parameters and results are clearly documented (C98). However, the relatively low consistency index (0.272) suggests substantial homoplasy in the dataset.

results.result: A clade comprising Eusaurosphargis and Palatodonta is recovered as the sister-group to Sauropterygia within the newly erected taxon Sauropterygomorpha. These taxa likely represent the morphology of the last common terrestrial ancestor of sauropterygians, supported by morphological features including small premaxilla, anteriorly positioned nares, hindlimb dominance, and shared foot morphology.
results.evaluation: The phylogenetic placement is supported by synapomorphies (C58-C62) and morphological evidence (C121-C122, C125-C126). The inference about terrestrial lifestyle is well-supported by multiple lines of evidence including limb proportions and bone microanatomy from cited literature. The suggestion that Palatodonta may be a junior synonym of Eusaurosphargis (C128) is appropriately presented as tentative, requiring additional specimens for confirmation.

results.result: The phylogenetic positions of several Early and Middle Triassic sauropterygians are clarified: Pomolispondylus is recovered as the most basal member of the grade leading to Eosauropterygia; Hanosaurus type and referred specimens are not recovered as monophyletic; Corosaurus is the earliest-diverging eosauropterygian; Wumengosaurus lies outside pachypleurosaurs + nothosaurs + pistosaurs; and Atopodentatus is sister to placodonts within Placodontiformes.
results.evaluation: The phylogenetic placements are supported by the analysis results and morphological comparisons (C134-C138). The recognition that the Hanosaurus type and referred specimens may represent different taxa (C104, C137-C138) is based on coracoid morphology differences documented in Figure 7. The placement of Pomolispondylus is supported by morphological features of dorsal transverse processes and osteoderm reduction (C134-C136). The Atopodentatus-placodont relationship is supported by four synapomorphies (C108).

results.result: The phylogenetic analysis supports placement of Testudines and Archosauromorpha within Archelosauria, along with the three major marine reptile clades (Sauropterygomorpha, Ichthyosauromorpha, Thalattosauria). This represents one of only two morphology-only analyses to recover this topology. Eunotosaurus is recovered outside Sauria, suggesting convergent evolution of turtle-like features.
results.evaluation: The recovery of Archelosauria is supported by four synapomorphies (C115) and is consistent with molecular data (C37). The placement of Eunotosaurus outside Sauria (C161) contradicts most recent morphological analyses but agrees with Simões et al. 2022. The inference of convergent evolution (C162) logically follows from this phylogenetic placement. However, the low consistency index and conflict with other morphological analyses suggest this result should be interpreted cautiously.

results.result: Prosaurosphargis extends the fossil record of Saurosphargidae back by approximately 3 Ma to the Early Triassic (Olenekian), making it the fourth major marine reptile lineage in the Nanzhang-Yuan'an fauna. The presence of multiple marine reptile lineages with diverse body sizes and ecologies in this fauna supports rapid diversification of sauropterygians in South China following the end-Smithian extinction.
results.evaluation: The stratigraphic age is well-documented (C49-C57, C67) and the temporal extension is supported by comparison with other saurosphargid occurrences (C40-C42, C116). The diversity of the Nanzhang-Yuan'an fauna is documented through multiple cited studies (C117). The inference of rapid diversification (C119, C151) is supported by the stratigraphic distribution of early sauropterygians (Figure 9) and is consistent with patterns in other marine reptile groups (C15-C16).

results.result: The phylogenetic topology reveals three key episodes in the evolution of the eosauropterygian body plan: (1) reduction of osteoderms and shortening of dorsal transverse processes (Pomolispondylus); (2) complete loss of osteoderms (Majiashanosaurus, Hanosaurus referred specimen); (3) evolution of emarginated coracoid morphology (Hanosaurus type specimen). Dermal armor was likely a preadaptation for marine colonization, with subsequent reduction associated with active predation and pelagic lifestyle.
results.evaluation: The evolutionary sequence is supported by the phylogenetic topology (Figure 8, 10) and morphological comparisons (C134-C138). The functional interpretations regarding dermal armor (C152-C154) are supported by cited biomechanical studies (C152) and are consistent with observed morphological patterns. The three-episode framework (C147-C150) provides a clear narrative supported by the phylogenetic distribution of character states.

results.result: The evolution of the sauropterygian body plan shows striking parallels with ichthyosaur evolution, with both lineages exhibiting dermal armor in early-diverging forms and subsequent loss associated with pelagic adaptation. This suggests dermal armor may have been a preadaptation for marine invasion in multiple diapsid clades.
results.evaluation: The parallel pattern in ichthyosaurs is supported by cited literature (C156-C157). However, the inference that dermal armor was a general preadaptation for marine invasion (C159) is speculative and marked as such in the evidence type. The pattern is observed in only two lineages, which is insufficient to establish a general principle. Additional data from other marine reptile lineages (thalattosaurs, as mentioned in the text) would be needed to support this broader claim.

results.result: The current phylogenetic analysis differs from Wang et al. 2022 due to more comprehensive taxonomic sampling (40 vs 16 outgroup taxa representing 23 vs 5 major lineages) and greater character sampling (221 vs 181 characters). The study emphasizes the importance of broad taxonomic sampling, including both terrestrial and aquatic outgroups, for accurate phylogenetic reconstruction.
results.evaluation: The methodological differences are clearly documented (C140-C141, C166-C167). The critique of limited outgroup sampling is supported by phylogenetic theory (C143, citing Wilberg 2015) and the importance of character sampling is supported by cited literature (C144, citing Wiens 2006). The specific criticism regarding the single terrestrial outgroup in Wang et al. 2022 (C142) is justified given the phylogenetic distance of Youngina from Sauropterygia (Figure 8).

results.result: Atopodentatus and early placodonts show high adaptation to aquatic lifestyle (humerus longer than femur) but retain features suggesting hindlimb importance for benthic/marginal locomotion (massive fourth trochanter, well-developed iliac blade). This may explain the absence of placodont fossils in the Early Triassic, with the specialized placodont body plan possibly not evolving until the Middle Triassic.
results.evaluation: The morphological observations are supported by cited literature (C129-C131). However, the explanation for the absence of Early Triassic placodonts (C132-C133) is explicitly marked as speculation. While the hypothesis is plausible and consistent with the phylogenetic placement of Atopodentatus, it requires additional fossil evidence to test. The authors appropriately acknowledge this limitation.

results.result: Helveticosaurus is recovered as the sister-group of Sauropterygomorpha, supported by six synapomorphies. However, it is interpreted as convergently evolving an aquatic lifestyle rather than being part of Sauropterygomorpha due to absence of osteoderms and potentially convergent carpal/tarsal features.
results.evaluation: The phylogenetic placement is supported by six synapomorphies (C112). The interpretation of convergent aquatic adaptation (C123) is reasonable given the absence of osteoderms (a key feature of Sauropterygomorpha) and the authors' acknowledgment that some shared features may represent aquatic adaptations. However, this interpretation involves some subjective judgment about character weighting and homology assessment.

results.result: The specimen originates from the upper part of the third member of the Jialingjiang Formation at Yingzishan quarry, representing the Nanzhang-Yuan'an fauna. The study adopts a three-member division of the Jialingjiang Formation based on recent geological mapping, with the thick volcanic ash marking the Lower-Middle Triassic boundary. The burial environment is interpreted as a restricted, stagnant, hypersaline lagoon within a tidal flat.
results.evaluation: The stratigraphic position is documented with geological maps and stratigraphic columns (Figure 1). The three-member division is supported by recent geological mapping (C53) and is consistent with official geological guides (C54) and regional volcanic ash markers (C55). The sedimentological interpretation (C57) is based on multiple published studies and field observations. The authors provide clear justification for their stratigraphic framework.

results.result: Sauropterygomorpha tax. nov. is diagnosed by five characters: presence of osteoderms, dorsoventrally flattened body, clavicle applied to medial surface of scapula, long and slender metatarsal V, and metatarsal I less than 50% the length of metatarsal IV.
results.evaluation: The diagnosis is based on the phylogenetic analysis and represents synapomorphies recovered for this clade. The characters are clearly defined and can be observed in the included taxa. This is a formal taxonomic act supported by the phylogenetic results.

results.result: The phylogenetic analysis used a modified version of the Qiao et al. 2022 data matrix, containing 57 OTUs scored for 221 characters. Ten OTUs were added to the original dataset. Parsimony analysis was performed in TNT 1.5 using a Traditional Search algorithm with all characters equally weighted and unordered.
results.evaluation: The methods are clearly documented and follow standard phylogenetic practices. The modifications to the original matrix are specified (C167), and the analysis parameters are provided (C168-C169). The approach is appropriate for the research question and allows for reproducibility.
